discovery: Discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube Neutrino Observatory
motivation: Francis Halzen conceived and led IceCube, the cubic-kilometre neutrino detector at the South Pole, which in 2013 established a diffuse flux of TeV-PeV neutrinos of extraterrestrial origin. This opened a new observational window on the high-energy universe. IceCube then found evidence for neutrino emission from the blazar TXS 0506+056 (2018) and the Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068 (2022), and observed neutrinos from the Galactic plane (2023). Neutrinos are produced only in hadronic interactions, so these results tie cosmic-ray acceleration directly to identified sources, which photons alone cannot do. The measurements are robust, have been confirmed in several independent channels, and now constrain models of cosmic-ray sources, of gamma-ray and neutrino production, and of neutrino properties at energies far beyond accelerators. Halzen's sustained theoretical vision and experimental leadership made neutrino astronomy a mature, quantitative field of physics.
